Q15.question: What are the most important open scientific challenges (by Feb 2026) in AI-based multiscale modeling of solid-state materials?

required_claims.text: Current challenges limiting AI-driven multiscale modeling include limited data availability, restricted model transferability, and limited explainability.

Artificial intelligence has transformed multiscale modeling by linking atomic, mesoscale, and continuum scales, delivering improved accuracy and reduced computational cost compared with traditional methods.

Machine-learning-driven interatomic potentials (e.g., GAP, DeePMD) and DFT-trained surrogate models enable simulations of up to millions of atoms while retaining accuracy close to first-principles benchmarks, making large-scale high-fidelity simulations feasible.

Neural-network-based electronic-structure prediction tools achieve significant speedups over conventional density-functional theory while maintaining comparable accuracy, accelerating electronic-structure calculations.
Graph neural network architectures such as MEGNet and SchNet enhance prediction of phase transitions, defect dynamics, and bulk material properties relative to classical computational approaches.
The multiscale structural complexity measure introduced by Bagrov et al. detects phase transitions in classical spin systems via a sharp extremum in the temperature derivative dC/dT.

Integrating renormalization-group concepts with machine-learning architectures has been used to predict transitions to canted antiferromagnetic phases in 3D Ising and Fermi-Hubbard models, to classify quantum phases, and to recognize complex many-body phases from raw simulation data.
Future integration of formal renormalization-group concepts with machine-learning architectures is a promising direction for modeling systems near criticality or with strong electron correlations.

The survey proposes a task-driven taxonomy that organizes foundation models into six application areas: data extraction/interpretation/Q&A, atomistic simulation, property prediction, materials structure/design/discovery, process planning/discovery/optimization, and multiscale modeling.

The Open Quantum Materials Database (OQMD) contains over 200,000 DFT-calculated crystal structures, including experimental ICSD entries and theoretical prototype structures, and is freely accessible to the scientific community without usage restrictions.

Q16.question: How does E(3)-equivariance improve GNN-based interatomic potentials in accuracy and data efficiency in comparison with vanilla GNN?

required_claims.text: NequIP achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on the MD-17 benchmark, surpassing invariant GNN-IPs, shallow neural networks, and kernel-based methods.
NequIP requires up to three orders of magnitude fewer training configurations than existing neural interatomic potentials to reach comparable accuracy.
Using higher-order E(3)-equivariant representations (increasing rotation order from l=0 to l=1 and up to l=3) consistently reduces prediction error and improves accuracy across all evaluated tasks.
DeepH-E3 attains sub-meV accuracy after training on only a few hundred DFT calculations of small, non-twisted structures, demonstrating high data efficiency.
NequIP outperforms kernel-based approaches such as sGDML and FCHL19/GPR across benchmarks, including small-data regimes and the MD-17 dataset.
When trained on only 133 structures (~1 k frames), NequIP outperforms DeepMD trained on 133,500 structures for liquid water and ice simulations.
Predicting forces as the negative gradient of the learned total energy guarantees energy conservation and rotation-equivariant forces.
The equivariant architecture scales linearly with the number of atoms because convolutions are limited to a local cutoff radius.
NequIP attains chemical-accuracy energy errors (~2 meV) on CCSD(T) benchmark molecules using only 1,000 reference configurations, outperforming sGDML and GemNet.
NequIP reproduces structural and kinetic properties from ab-initio molecular dynamics simulations with high fidelity.

Q17.question: Give evidences that ML-based coarse-grained molecular dynamics is effective for studying ionic transport and phase transitions in solid-state systems (by Feb 2026).

required_claims.text: Graph neural network architectures such as MEGNet and SchNet enhance prediction of phase transitions, defect dynamics, and bulk material properties relative to classical computational approaches.
The multiscale structural complexity measure introduced by Bagrov et al. detects phase transitions in classical spin systems via a sharp extremum in the temperature derivative dC/dT.

LiFlow achieves speed-ups of up to ~600,000× over ab initio molecular dynamics (and ~400× over MLIP), predicting a 1 ns trajectory in 48 s for a 2 × 2 × 1 LGPS supercell and 352 s for a 4 × 4 × 4 supercell.
The computational cost of LiFlow scales linearly with the number of atoms (O(n)), in contrast to the cubic scaling (O(n3)) of ab initio molecular dynamics.

LiFlow trained on 25 ps ab initio molecular dynamics trajectories can generate stable trajectories up to 1 ns in larger (4 × 4 × 4) supercells, reproducing lithium self-diffusivity, activation energies, and temperature dependence comparable to long AIMD simulations.
Fifth-order Gaussian quadrature yields internal energies and free-energy curves that remain in good agreement with molecular dynamics results across the full temperature range studied.

The E(3)-equivariant GNN surrogate provides superior accuracy compared with third- and fifth-order Gaussian quadrature for thermal expansion of copper, martensitic phase transition of iron, and grain-boundary energy calculations, matching molecular dynamics reference data.

Training U-MLIPs on energies, forces, and stresses yields the most physically accurate potential, with stresses required for modeling structural phase transformations or NPT ensemble molecular dynamics.

The proposed screening method is approximately 50 × faster than molecular dynamics driven by a machine-learning interatomic potential and at least 3 000 × faster than first-principles molecular dynamics.
The DeePMD model provides excellent energy conservation in all tested systems up to 2 ns of NVE dynamics.

The multiscale structural complexity measure introduced by Bagrov et al. detects phase transitions in classical spin systems via a sharp extremum in the temperature derivative dC/dT.

LiFlow achieves speed-ups of up to ~600,000× over ab initio molecular dynamics (and ~400× over MLIP), predicting a 1 ns trajectory in 48 s for a 2 × 2 × 1 LGPS supercell and 352 s for a 4 × 4 × 4 supercell.
The computational cost of LiFlow scales linearly with the number of atoms (O(n)), in contrast to the cubic scaling (O(n3)) of ab initio molecular dynamics.

LiFlow trained on 25 ps ab initio molecular dynamics trajectories can generate stable trajectories up to 1 ns in larger (4 × 4 × 4) supercells, reproducing lithium self-diffusivity, activation energies, and temperature dependence comparable to long AIMD simulations.

CHGNet molecular dynamics simulations of Li superionic conductors reproduce room-temperature ionic conductivities and activation energies within the error bars of AIMD, correctly distinguishing faster from slower conductors.

In charge-informed molecular dynamics of Li0.5MnO2 at 1100 K, CHGNet predicts the emergence of Mn2+ after ~0.8 ns, coinciding with a ~50 meV/oxygen reduction in potential energy and the formation of a spinel-like phase, indicating a correlation between charge disproportionation and phase transformation.
Fifth-order Gaussian quadrature yields internal energies and free-energy curves that remain in good agreement with molecular dynamics results across the full temperature range studied.

The E(3)-equivariant GNN surrogate provides superior accuracy compared with third- and fifth-order Gaussian quadrature for thermal expansion of copper, martensitic phase transition of iron, and grain-boundary energy calculations, matching molecular dynamics reference data.

Training U-MLIPs on energies, forces, and stresses yields the most physically accurate potential, with stresses required for modeling structural phase transformations or NPT ensemble molecular dynamics.

Q18.question: What mechanisms embed physical constraints, i.e., symmetry, locality, and size extensivity, into machine-learned interatomic potential architectures, and what evidence bears on whether these constraints improve transfer to system sizes and conditions beyond the training set (by Feb 2026)?

required_claims.text: A training database of manageable size, constructed from DFT configurations covering relevant phases and defects, is sufficient to achieve high transferability of the GAP model across diverse silicon configurations.
M3GNet potential covers 89 elements with no particular constraints on applicability, though training has strong bias toward solid phases.

Training set cleaning procedures including minimum ion-ion distance cutoff, energy/force outlier removal, and loss condition monitoring are necessary to help the algorithm converge to a physical model.

The proposed training protocol based on augmenting the training set via intermediate molecular dynamics simulations can assess the quality of approximate trajectories and computed physical properties.

For a MgO test set, M3GNet outperforms Moment Tensor Potentials in extrapolating equation-of-state behavior beyond the training regime and exhibits long-range interaction characteristics similar to a Buckingham + Coulomb model.

Unconstrained machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) trained on large datasets achieve accuracies on par with state-of-the-art equivariant architectures while maintaining orders-of-magnitude lower computational cost than quantum-mechanical methods.

Fine-tuning models pre-trained on OMat24 to the MAD dataset achieves near-converged validation metrics in 30-100 epochs versus 700+ epochs when training from scratch, halving validation energy and force errors and achieving 50% lower test error than training on MAD alone.

The PET architecture scales to 730M parameters (OMat-XL) while maintaining tractable memory usage and computational efficiency due to increased node representation size and unconstrained architecture.

Non-conservative models allow residual asymmetries to drive relaxation toward more stable close-packed structures, unlike equivariant models that remain trapped in symmetric but unstable configurations, though 70% (16%) of final configurations retain symmetry of initial structure with 0.01 Å threshold for conservative (non-conservative) models.

Elastic moduli predictions are very sensitive to the lack of energy conservation in MLIP models, and non-conservative models consistently perform worse on matbench-discovery downstream tasks despite achieving better training and validation accuracies.
